title: Review: Gibbs free energy and feasibility; Rate equations and orders; Arrhenius equation; Concentration–time graphs, half-life and clock reactions; Rate-determining step and mechanisms
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: KN04#t3 term and clue written for the game; KN04#t1 term and clue written for the game; KN04#t2 term and clue written for the game; KN06#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EN09#N.5, KN04#N.6a, KN05#N.12b, KN06#N.3a, KN07#N.12, KN04#N.3a, KN05#N.11, KN06#N.8, KN07#N.3, KN07#N.13a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Rate equation
items.clue: Expression such as k[X][Y] that links how fast a reaction goes to concentrations.

items.label: Order
items.clue: The power to which a reactant's concentration is raised; found only by experiment.

items.label: Rate constant
items.clue: The proportionality factor, k; it changes with temperature but not with concentration.

items.label: Transition state
items.clue: Sits at an energy maximum, with bonds partly made and partly broken; cannot be isolated.

questions.stem: For C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g), calculate ΔG at 298 K. ΔH = −136 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −120.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Answers in kJ mol⁻¹.
The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A]², with concentrations in mol dm⁻³ and the rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. What are the units of k?

options.text: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, as the rate constant has the same units as the rate
mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹, as k = rate/[A]² for a second-order reaction
s⁻¹, as only one reactant, A, appears in the rate equation
mol³ dm⁻⁹ s⁻¹, as k = rate × [A]² when the rate equation is rearranged

questions.explanation: (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹, for any reaction that is second order overall.

questions.stem: A hypothetical compound X decomposes at constant temperature. Three runs give these initial rates. - [X] / mol dm⁻³: 0.160, 0.320, 0.640. Initial rate / mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹: 5.60 × 10⁻⁴, 1.12 × 10⁻³, 2.24 × 10⁻³. - What are the order with respect to X and the rate constant, k?

options.text: Second order; k = 2.19 × 10⁻² dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
First order; k = 2.86 × 10² s
First order; k = 3.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹
First order; k = 3.50 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

questions.explanation: Rate ×2 when [X] ×2: first order. k = 5.60 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 0.160 = 3.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ (same from every run).

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a reaction intermediate from a transition state in a multistep reaction?

options.text: A transition state can be isolated if the reaction is stopped quickly enough, just as an intermediate can.
An intermediate is present at the start and is re-formed at the end; a transition state is used up.
An intermediate lies at an energy minimum between steps; a transition state is at a maximum and cannot be isolated.
An intermediate appears in the overall equation for the reaction; a transition state does not.

questions.explanation: The intermediate sits in a dip, so it lasts long enough to be detected in principle. The transition state is a peak.

questions.stem: Reactions 1 and 2 have the same Arrhenius factor, A. Reaction 1 has the larger activation energy. Both are plotted as ln k against 1/T on the same axes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Reaction 1's line is less steep, as a larger Ea makes k less sensitive to temperature.
The lines are parallel, with reaction 1's line lower, as Ea only shifts the line down.
Reaction 1's line has a positive gradient, as its k rises faster with temperature.
Reaction 1's line is steeper, and both lines meet the ln k axis at one point.

questions.explanation: Larger Ea, steeper line. Intercept = ln A, the same for both.

questions.stem: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A][B]². At constant temperature, the concentrations of A and B are both doubled. By what factor does the rate increase?
questions.explanation: Doubling [A] gives ×2¹ = 2; doubling [B] gives ×2² = 4. The rate rises by 2 × 4 = 8.

questions.stem: In an iodine clock, the blue-black colour appears after 48 s. A second run uses double the concentration of I⁻, with everything else the same, and the colour appears after 24 s. What is the order with respect to I⁻?

options.text: Zero order, as the same amount of iodine forms in both runs.
Order −1, as the time halves when [I⁻] doubles.
Second order, as [I⁻] doubles and the time halves: a factor of 2 × 2.
First order, as 1/t doubles when [I⁻] doubles.

questions.explanation: Rate ∝ 1/t. Doubling [I⁻] doubles 1/t, so the rate is proportional to [I⁻]: first order.

questions.stem: The overall equation for a reaction is 2X + Y → X₂Y. The experimental rate equation is rate = k[X][Y]. Which mechanism is consistent with both?

options.text: Step 1: X + Y → XY (slow). Step 2: XY + X → X₂Y (fast).
Step 1: X + X → X₂ (slow). Step 2: X₂ + Y → X₂Y (fast).
Step 1: X + Y ⇌ XY (fast). Step 2: XY + X → X₂Y (slow).
Step 1: X + Y → XY (slow). Step 2: XY + Y → XY₂ (fast).

questions.explanation: The steps add to 2X + Y → X₂Y, and the slow first step has one X and one Y: rate = k[X][Y].

questions.stem: For a reaction with Ea = 50 kJ mol⁻¹, raising the temperature from 300 K to 310 K almost doubles the rate. Which statement gives the main reason for this large increase?

options.text: A much larger fraction of all the collisions now have energy equal to or greater than Ea.
The particles move faster, so they collide more often, and more collisions give more reactions.
The activation energy decreases as the temperature rises, so more of the collisions succeed.
Every particle gains the same amount of energy, which carries many more of them past Ea.

questions.stem: A clock reaction is timed at several temperatures, with the same starting concentrations each time. Rate ∝ 1/t, so ln(1/t) stands in for ln k. On a plot of ln(1/t) against 1/T / 10⁻³ K⁻¹, two points on the line are (3.10, −2.30) and (3.40, −4.25). What is Ea? R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

options.text: 0.782 kJ mol⁻¹
54.0 kJ mol⁻¹
6.50 kJ mol⁻¹
0.0540 kJ mol⁻¹
